variants.name: sync.OnceValues-backed getter (value and error cached)
variants.implementation_notes: Go's standard library supplies the guard: sync.OnceValues(loader) returns a function that runs the loader exactly once and returns the cached (value, error) on later calls, which matches a fallible store read; sync.OnceValue is the single-value sibling. The holder is a struct field of function type (or the once plus result fields when the loader needs arguments), and the accessor method is where first touch happens because the language has no attribute hooks.
pitfalls: sync.OnceValues caches the error as well as the value: a transient database failure is returned forever unless the loader retries internally or the holder can be reset.
A cached nil is indistinguishable from 'not loaded'; represent an absent row explicitly (sql.ErrNoRows or a sentinel value) so callers can tell absence from deferral.
Once state travels with the function value: copying the struct or rebuilding the closure per call re-runs the load, and the same once must never be shared between different rows.

variants.name: Hand-written loaded flag under sync.Mutex
variants.implementation_notes: The hand-written classic: the struct keeps a sync.Mutex, a loaded flag and the value; the getter locks, checks the flag, calls the loader and stores the result. Choose it when the loader needs runtime arguments (a single closure cannot serve several keys), when a failed load must be retryable (once semantics would swallow the retry) or when the code predates Go 1.21; sync.Once is the middle ground when the loader takes no arguments.
variants.idiom_name: loaded flag + sync.Mutex (or sync.Once) holder method
pitfalls: Holding the lock across the loader serializes every reader of that object; if the load does I/O this blocks unrelated goroutines, and a loader that re-enters Author() self-deadlocks.
A holder containing a mutex must not be copied after first use (go vet copylocks flags it); keep holders behind pointers.
